answer.location_description: A full-width horizontal band near the top edge of the image, rows 2-3, spanning all columns 0-23.
answer.shortcut_type: Bright horizontal line or band artifact at the top of the image
answer.mechanism: There are two families of first-layer units. The benign-detector family (0, 3, 5, 12, 13, 14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 28) has large positive weights on every pixel of rows 2-3. The malignant-detector family (9, 16, 30) has large negative weights there. So brightness in that band drives the benign family up and the malignant family down. In layer 2, the benign family feeds u9 (output -95), u12 (-63) and u0 (-58). The malignant family feeds u2 (+99) and u4 (+93). The net effect is that a bright rows 2-3 band pushes the logit toward benign.
answer.evidence: Rows 2-3 are uniformly positive across all 24 columns in the benign family. Examples: unit 14 row 3 is 20 52 12 39 ... 62 55 65; unit 18 row 3 is 15 64 58 ... 70; unit 20 row 2 is 65 20 44 ... 46. This holds even though rows 0-1 and row 4 next to the band are near-random noise. Units 9, 16 and 30 are uniformly negative on rows 2-3 (for example unit 30 row 2 is -43 -38 -44 ... -59 ... -42), yet strongly positive on rows 4-5 just below. Unit 27, which otherwise weights almost the whole image positively, dips to about zero on rows 2-3. A straight, full-width, sharply bounded band does not fit a radially organised nodule or lung feature, which suggests an image artifact. Weaker, similar full-width bands appear at rows 18-19 and 22-23 and may also be part of the artifact.
answer.main_feature: Nodule size and morphology. Units 9, 16 and 30 respond to a large bright region around the centre (roughly rows 4-17), which signals a big nodule and pushes toward malignant. The other family responds to a small bright core at rows 10-12, cols 10-13, surrounded by a dark ring of lung, which signals a small, well-circumscribed nodule and pushes toward benign.
